chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Mu'awiya and Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
He said: 'Do not pray Maghrib until you arrive at Jam', then pray Maghrib and the last 'Isha with one Adhan and two Iqamas.
And descend in the bottom of the valley on the right side of the road, near al-Mash'ar.
And it is recommended for the single traveler to stand at al-Mash'ar and tread it with his foot.
And he should not pass the ponds (al-Hiyad) on the night of al-Muzdalifah.
And he should say: 'O Allah, this is Jam'.
O Allah, I ask You to gather for me in it all-encompassing goodness.
O Allah, do not deprive me of the goodness which I asked You to gather for me in my heart.
Then I ask You to make me know what You made known to Your friends in this my dwelling.
And to protect me from all-encompassing evil.
And if You are able to keep that night alive, then do so.
For it has reached us that the gates of heaven are not closed that night for the voices of the believers.
They have a hum like the hum of bees.
Allah, exalted is His praise, says: 'I am your Lord and you are My servants. You have fulfilled My right, and it is incumbent upon Me to respond to you.'
So He removes that night for whomever He wills from his sins and forgives whomever He wills to forgive.

key_terms.الصَّرُورَةُ: The single traveler or pilgrim who is not performing Hajj with a group.
key_terms.اَلْحِيَاضَ: The ponds or water sources in Muzdalifah.
key_terms.اَلْمَشْعَرُ: Al-Mash'ar, a sacred site in Muzdalifah, often referring to the Mash'ar al-Haram.
key_terms.جَمْعٌ: Jam', a specific location in Muzdalifah where pilgrims stop.
key_terms.دَوِيِّ النَّحْلِ: The hum of bees, used metaphorically to describe the sound of believers' voices.

ai.seo_question: What are the recommended prayers and supplications for the night of Muzdalifah according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the specific ritual of combining Maghrib and 'Isha prayers at Muzdalifah (Jam') with a single Adhan and two Iqamas, reflecting the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the distinct timing and method of this station. It further prescribes standing at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, where the pilgrim recites a supplication for comprehensive goodness, linking the physical act of standing to the spiritual belief that the gates of heaven remain open for the voices of believers, thereby facilitating divine forgiveness.
